title: The Pawnee Eagleton Tip Off Classic

jokes.text: Okay, here's the text I added a few more jokes, slamming Eagleton at the end. / Mmm. That's the sexiest thing you've ever said to me.
jokes.setup: Ben presents a press conference text with Eagleton-bashing additions — mundane political task
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response treats political mudslinging as an intimate, romantic act
jokes.explanation: The joke perfectly captures Leslie's all-consuming political passion bleeding into her personal life. Her treating anti-Eagleton rhetoric as pillow talk is very on-brand, and it lands as a strong cold-open beat. Character-specific and well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, Ben. Keep going. This is... this is really turning me on.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? We're just talking about Eagleton's failed infrastructure initiatives.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know. It's so hot. More. Tell me about their wasteful spending.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Uh, their parks department is severely underfunded compared to—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes! Yes! Oh god, yes!

jokes.text: Am I proud of it? Yes. Because Eagleton sucks. But is it the classiest move? Yes, because Eagleton sucks. Would I do it again? Yes, because Eagleton sucks.
jokes.setup: Leslie is asked if she's sure she wants to attack Eagleton at the press conference
jokes.punchline: She runs through all three rhetorical self-questioning options — proud? classy? do again? — and collapses each one into the same triumphant answer
jokes.explanation: The tricolon structure with identical punchlines is a classic comedy technique executed beautifully here. Leslie's self-interrogation that always returns to 'Eagleton sucks' subverts the form of reasonable self-reflection. High quotability. One of the episode's stronger bits.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Did I attack Eagleton? Yes. Was I justified? Yes. Would I do it again? Yes. Should I have done it differently? Yes, but still yes.

jokes.text: That awful human being is Ingrid de Forest. She's a city councilor from Eagleton. She thinks she's so great because she won the Miss Indiana Beauty Pageant. Last year. While she was in office. And pregnant.
jokes.setup: Leslie introduces her Eagleton rival in a confessional talking head
jokes.punchline: Each successive detail (last year, while in office, and pregnant) escalates the absurdity of Leslie's resentment — the accomplishments she's listing are actually impressive, making Leslie's hatred funnier
jokes.explanation: The escalating reveal structure is perfectly deployed. The comedy comes from the dawning realization that Leslie's grievances are actually inadvertent compliments — winning a beauty pageant while pregnant and in office is legitimately impressive. Leslie's obliviousness to this irony is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ingrid is so stuck-up. She thinks she's better than everyone else.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: She went to Yale.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: She was captain of the rowing team.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: She speaks four languages.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: She's been published in The New Yorker.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, actually, she IS better than everyone else.

jokes.text: Ew, pesticide. Yuck. / Oh, no, these are pesticide-free. I ate one of these for breakfast this morning, and I found a worm in it. / So, I bet somebody feels pretty stupid right now.
jokes.setup: Ingrid sneers at Pawnee's apple basket as a wager, assuming it's full of pesticides
jokes.punchline: Leslie corrects her — they're pesticide-free — but the correction reveals an equally unappealing alternative (a worm). Leslie then triumphantly declares victory in the exchange.
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke: the correction itself is funny (pesticide-free but wormy), and Leslie's triumphant 'somebody feels pretty stupid' is a great character beat — she's genuinely proud of an argument she lost. Solid mid-tier joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: I can't eat these apples. They're covered in pesticides.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I washed them myself. See? Pesticide-free.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: You washed them in what?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Motor oil. It cuts right through the pesticides.

jokes.text: Of course, it's silly to compare apples and oranges, but what the heck. These are made of Swarovski crystal, and they're worth $700,000.
jokes.setup: Ingrid casually remarks it's silly to compare apples and oranges (using the idiom) before presenting Eagleton's counter-wager
jokes.punchline: The oranges are made of Swarovski crystal worth $700,000 — the idiom becomes literal absurdism reflecting Eagleton's obscene wealth
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The wordplay on 'apples and oranges' sets up a pun, but the payoff goes far beyond the pun into world-building absurdism ($700,000 crystal oranges). The idiom usage as both literal and figurative simultaneously is clever double-layered writing. Strong originality.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: So you're telling me Eagleton's oranges are worth a fortune?

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: That's right. Our oranges are superior in every way.

jokes.text: I'll tell you what I'd do if I was an Eagletonian. I'd pop a Xanax and ask my butler to help me out.
jokes.setup: Reporter asks Leslie what she'd do to make up a 15-point poll deficit
jokes.punchline: Leslie pivots to mocking Eagleton's privileged lifestyle as her answer — the joke is that she can't answer a question about herself without making it about Eagleton
jokes.explanation: Functional joke that characterizes Leslie's obsession with Eagleton-bashing, but the Xanax/butler punchline is fairly predictable class-warfare humor. The character work is good; the actual gag is mid-tier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I would immediately adopt an affected accent, join a country club, and spend my days judging people who shop at regular grocery stores.

jokes.text: When you tell 'em it's time to change their oil, they ask, 'Extra virgin or white truffle?'
jokes.setup: Leslie continues her press conference mockery of Eagletonians being out of touch
jokes.punchline: They mistake motor oil for cooking oil — the specific choices (extra virgin, white truffle) elevate the joke from generic to precise
jokes.explanation: The specific detail of 'extra virgin or white truffle' elevates what could be a generic rich-people joke. Economy is excellent — the punchline does a lot with few words. A well-crafted quick joke in the press conference riff.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: They confuse motor oil with fancy cooking oil

jokes.text: Unless, of course, you're an Eagletonian, and then you'll be too busy polishing your monocle at the caviar store. Knope out.
jokes.setup: Leslie wraps up her press conference remarks
jokes.punchline: She signs off with a final Eagleton jab ('polishing your monocle at the caviar store') and then delivers 'Knope out' as a triumphant mic-drop
jokes.explanation: 'Knope out' is a great character-specific mic-drop that gets a laugh on its own. The monocle/caviar store gag is stock rich-people comedy, but 'Knope out' as a genuine exit brand elevates the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: See you at the game

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I can't make it. I have to go polo with some hedge fund managers and then we're taking the private jet to our summer home in the Hamptons.

jokes.text: This was sent to Ron Swanson at Diane's address, where I've lived for less than a month. How is that possible? This is an extreme invasion of privacy.
jokes.setup: Ron is outraged about receiving a Penny Saver coupon circular at his new home
jokes.punchline: Ron treats a junk mail circular as an 'extreme invasion of privacy' — his libertarian paranoia is wildly disproportionate to the minor annoyance
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron: his privacy obsession is always the source of his best material. The junk mail vs. 'extreme invasion of privacy' gap is well-calibrated. Strong character integration — this is entirely a Ron joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: My father accidentally subscribed to Ebony magazine instead of some hunting and fishing publication. Best thing that ever happened to us. Very educational.

jokes.text: My family has had a single P.O. box for several generations. We only ever subscribe to two magazines, Reader's Digest and Ebony. Ebony was due to a clerical error, but it ended up being an interesting year of reading.
jokes.setup: Ron explains his family's extreme privacy philosophy around mail and subscriptions
jokes.punchline: Ebony arriving via clerical error, then being described as 'an interesting year of reading' — the deadpan acceptance and mild surprise is quintessential Ron
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: P.O. box for generations → Reader's Digest → Ebony (clerical error) → 'interesting year of reading.' Each beat builds. The total non-racism of Ron's reaction (he just found it interesting) combined with the deadpan delivery makes it genuinely surprising. Strong character integration — only Ron would describe this experience in these exact terms.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Donna's got this incredible talent for mailing lists. She can organize any list faster than anyone I've ever seen.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: But me? I've got my own thing. I'm addicted to oven mitts with puns on them. I've got like 200 pairs at home.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: My favorite one says 'That's a Mitt!' Like, 'That's a mitt!' Get it?

jokes.text: She got me off the Williams-Sonoma mailing list, but then I just signed back up again. Hooked on their oven mitts. I need my mitts on those mitts.
jokes.setup: Jerry/Garry recommends Donna for getting off mailing lists, mentioning she got him off Williams-Sonoma
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts the recommendation — he signed back up because of oven mitt addiction. 'I need my mitts on those mitts' is a silly self-aware wordplay capper.
jokes.explanation: A nice quick joke that lands on 'I need my mitts on those mitts' — a wordplay that almost works by accident, making it funnier. Jerry's gentle self-undermining is in character. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Donna's at the Coffee Baru on 5th Street right now. She checked in on Yelp three minutes ago.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Based on her Twitter activity pattern, she'll be there for exactly 12 more minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Then she's heading to the DMV. I can tell because she always complains about the DMV on Instagram between 2 and 2:15.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I've mapped her entire afternoon using social media. I'm basically a digital bloodhound.

jokes.text: According to her Twitter feed, she got coffee five minutes ago. Wait, now she's Ustreaming her walk back. She should be here in three, two, one.
jokes.setup: Ron asks to be notified when Donna returns
jokes.punchline: Tom tracks Donna's location via her social media in real time and counts her down to the second — paying off immediately when Donna walks in
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff is excellent — Tom counting down and Donna walking in on 'one' is a perfectly timed visual/structural joke. Character integration is good (Tom's social media obsession). The realization that Tom has been tracking her every movement is funny in a slightly creepy way.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I know about the tracking. I've been adding fake locations to throw you off.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Because it's fun watching you stress about where I am. Plus, I'm documenting everything you do too. I've got three binders.

jokes.text: Hey, hey. Hashtag quest for coffee, blowin' up my timeline. You get my snapchat about it? / No. / What? / There it is.
jokes.setup: Donna arrives back from getting coffee, excited about her social media documentation of the event
jokes.punchline: Tom didn't get the Snapchat, which momentarily devastates Donna — then 'There it is' as the Snapchat finally arrives, completing a tiny tech drama
jokes.explanation: Fun character moment for Donna and Tom. The beat of Tom not getting the Snapchat and then 'There it is' is a nice quick structural joke. A little dated now (Ustream, early Snapchat) but functional for its era.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Hey, catch!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Got it! Thanks, Susan.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You named your calculator Susan?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Well, yeah. It helps me stay organized.

jokes.text: Think fast. / Oh, my God. / Hey, Dr. Buttons-- I mean, my old calculator. It doesn't have a name.
jokes.setup: Ben throws a calculator at Chris to get his attention
jokes.punchline: Chris almost calls it 'Dr. Buttons' before catching himself and claiming it has no name — revealing he has named and emotionally bonded with a calculator
jokes.explanation: A perfectly constructed quick joke. The reveal that Chris named his calculator 'Dr. Buttons' and then poorly covers for it is a great character moment — it tells us something specific and delightful about Chris. The economy is excellent: 'it doesn't have a name' is the funniest possible way to try to walk it back.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I've been brushing up on my math skills. You know, for the accounting work.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's great, Chris.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Yeah, I've been thinking of myself as Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid, except it's Butch Casually and the Sum-dance Kid.

jokes.text: Butch Count-sidy and the Sum-dance Kid, together again.
jokes.setup: Ben proposes that he and Chris work together on the Eagleton budget audit
jokes.punchline: Ben delivers a perfectly constructed accounting pun on 'Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid' — Count-sidy (counting) and Sum-dance (sum/math)
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best pure joke. The double pun on 'Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid' with 'Count-sidy' and 'Sum-dance' is remarkably well-constructed — both halves of the title are independently punned on accounting/math concepts, and it's delivered with the casual confidence of someone who's been waiting to use it. High quotability. Strong character integration (Ben is the former city manager turned finance nerd). Economy is nearly perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Auditing is going to be AMAZING! We're gonna crush it, bro! We're gonna be lean, mean, budgeting machines! Gonna optimize every dollar, every cent, maximize efficiency across the board!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Wait, I need to rephrase that in a more inclusive way. We're going to be lean, mean, budgeting... colleagues. We're going to optimize every dollar and cent together as an inclusive team of diverse backgrounds and perspectives!

jokes.text: Auditing bros! / Yeah, and auditing sistah. Let's do this.
jokes.setup: Ben and Chris celebrate their reunion as an auditing duo
jokes.punchline: Leslie inserts herself into their bromance celebration with 'auditing sistah' — the joke is her mild jealousy and need to be included
jokes.explanation: A quick functional joke — Leslie's need to insert herself is in character, and it's a decent capper to the Butch Count-sidy joke. But it's not especially original or memorable on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: If you have to take out a second mortgage to buy breakfast cereal, you might be from Eagleton.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: If your orange juice costs more than a used car, you might be from Eagleton.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: If your toast is made from artisanal bread that's flown in from Belgium and costs $47 a slice, you might be from Eagleton.

jokes.text: Oh, you're coming? / If there's a problem with Eagleton, I wanna be there. That's like a dream come true.
jokes.setup: Ben and Chris plan to go audit Eagleton; Leslie announces she's coming
jokes.punchline: Ben's slightly exasperated 'Oh, you're coming?' followed by Leslie treating witnessing Eagleton's financial crisis as 'a dream come true'
jokes.explanation: A mild joke that characterizes Leslie's gleeful antipathy toward Eagleton. 'Dream come true' is a good tag, but the setup is fairly weak. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We're going to Bloomington for baby supplies because Pawnee's baby store is right next to the old tire fire.

jokes.text: If you make your omelet out of Faberge eggs, you just might... / Be an Eagletonian.
jokes.setup: Leslie announces she has a new Jeff Foxworthy-style 'You might be an Eagletonian' routine in the car
jokes.punchline: First joke of the routine: Faberge egg omelet = Eagletonian. Ben completes the punchline format.
jokes.explanation: The Foxworthy parody structure is a fun framework for Leslie's Eagleton obsession. Faberge egg omelet is a good specific detail. The joke works both as a joke and as a character moment — Ben completing her punchline shows their relationship dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I made a playlist for the trip!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh no.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's all classical music and ambient sounds. I think we should have a sophisticated road trip experience.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Andy, you once ate an entire wheel of cheese in one sitting.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That was old Andy. New Andy appreciates the finer things.

jokes.text: Who's excited to go to Bloomington? / Is that where you're gonna sit? I'm driving. Where else would I sit? / Trunk.
jokes.setup: Ann cheerfully announces the road trip to Bloomington; April is in the front passenger seat
jokes.punchline: April's deadpan suggestion that Ann should sit in the trunk — delivered as a genuine alternative
jokes.explanation: Pure economy — 'Trunk' as a one-word punchline is perfect. April's hostility toward Ann is well-established, and the deadpan single word perfectly captures her character. Not particularly original but executed flawlessly.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Where else would I sit?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: The trunk.

jokes.text: I would get one in Pawnee, but fun fact -- our only baby store is attached to a chemical refinery.
jokes.setup: Ann explains why she needs to go to Bloomington for an organic baby blanket
jokes.punchline: Pawnee's only baby store is attached to a chemical refinery — a dark callback to the show's running joke about Pawnee being a terrible, toxic place
jokes.explanation: A well-executed Pawnee-is-terrible joke. The juxtaposition of 'organic baby blanket' with 'chemical refinery next door' is sharp, and it's delivered as a casual 'fun fact.' Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: I find discussing money to be terribly inappropriate. My family never spoke about finances at the dinner table.

jokes.text: Say cheese. / Damn it. You look beautiful.
jokes.setup: Leslie takes a photo of Ingrid, presumably hoping for an unflattering result
jokes.punchline: The photo turns out to be beautiful — Leslie's attempt to diminish her rival fails and she's forced to admit it
jokes.explanation: A visual/reaction gag that plays well. 'Damn it. You look beautiful' is a great character moment — Leslie's involuntary honesty despite her desire to hate Ingrid. Strong economy and character work.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: Here you go.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Oh, thank you! What's this?

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: Just a little something for your trouble.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Uh... this is Monopoly money.

jokes.text: We don't really like to talk about money. We find it a little gauche. / This is a budget meeting.
jokes.setup: Ben asks about Eagleton's budget deficits at the meeting
jokes.punchline: Ingrid demurs because discussing money is 'gauche' — she is at a budget meeting specifically about their financial crisis
jokes.explanation: Clean ironic joke — discussing money is gauche, at a budget meeting, because they're broke. Ben's flat 'This is a budget meeting' is the perfect straight-man response. Economy and structure are both strong.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm going to get off the grid. No phone, no email, no internet.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Ron, my entire romantic life depends on social media. I need you to stay connected.

jokes.text: Are you tipping me? Is that 100... Euros?
jokes.setup: After the meeting, Ingrid apparently hands Ben money, which he receives with bewilderment
jokes.punchline: Ingrid tips the auditor (who is a government official doing a budget audit), and the money is in Euros — reflecting both her condescending classism and her disconnect from American norms
jokes.explanation: Two-layered joke: the condescension of tipping a government official, plus the Euros detail that implies Ingrid is so cosmopolitan she doesn't carry dollars. Both layers work efficiently. Good character-building for Ingrid as an archetype.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The grid is good, the grid is great, we surrender our will as of this date.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: The grid is good, the grid is great, we surrender our will as of this date.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The grid is bad, the grid is wack, please everybody turn back.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: The grid is bad, the grid is wack, please everybody turn back.

jokes.text: I live for the grid. It's where I meet 40% of my jump-offs.
jokes.setup: Ron explains he wants to get completely off the grid
jokes.punchline: Donna's opposition is entirely self-interested — she meets 40% of her 'jump-offs' (casual hookups) online
jokes.explanation: A great Donna moment. '40% of my jump-offs' is the perfect Donna-speak — casual, specific, entirely unapologetic. The specificity of 40% makes it funnier than if she'd just said 'most.' Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I have a sleeping bag, a cooler full of raw meat, and a binder labeled 'Things I Know About Birds.' So yes, I'm prepared.

jokes.text: And if you're off the grid, how are you gonna post photos of the dope food at restaurants you're at and all the cool places you're stuntin' in?
jokes.setup: Ron wants to go off the grid; Tom argues against it
jokes.punchline: Tom's argument against privacy is entirely about social media documentation of food and 'stuntin'' — he's arguing for surveillance capitalism on purely aesthetic grounds
jokes.explanation: Functional Tom joke — his social-media-obsessed character is well-served here. But the observation about food posting is a bit broad. The 'stuntin'' usage is period-specific but in-character. Mid-tier.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm April Ludgate. I'm interested in majoring in assisted suicide.

dialogue.speaker: College Guide
dialogue.line: I... I'm sorry?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Assisted suicide. Dr. Kevorkian is my role model. Well, him and maybe a young Mussolini.

jokes.text: Grid, grid, grid, grid, grid, grid, grid-- / If you help me get off the grid, I will let both of you go home early. / No grid, no grid, no grid, no grid.
jokes.setup: Tom is chanting 'grid' to argue against Ron going off the grid; Ron offers an incentive
jokes.punchline: The instant Donna hears 'go home early,' she switches her chant from 'grid' to 'no grid' mid-sentence — pure mercenary pragmatism
jokes.explanation: Great structural joke — the escalating chant reversed instantly on hearing 'go home early' is a perfect Donna character moment. The structure (build up chant → incentive → reverse chant) is cleanly executed. It's about what Donna actually values: freedom over principle.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why would you leave me alone with the nice college guide? You know I'm going to kill her.

jokes.text: Yeah, an empty Sprite can, an old man's fingernail in my pocket, and a picture of Patrick Ewing on a roller coaster. I'm all set.
jokes.setup: Ann asks if April has everything she needs for vet school orientation
jokes.punchline: April lists her orientation supplies: an empty Sprite can, an old man's fingernail, and a Patrick Ewing roller coaster photo — all deeply wrong and bizarre
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's funniest pure absurdist joke. Each item is independently bizarre: the Sprite can is mundanely empty, the fingernail is grotesque, and Patrick Ewing on a roller coaster is an oddly specific celebrity image. Together they form a perfect portrait of April's chaotic inner world. Very high character integration — this list is uniquely, completely April. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Eagleton has some serious fiscal issues. Their budget is completely out of balance, their infrastructure is crumbling, and they're facing a potential downgrade in their bond rating. It's really quite dire. But you know what? I just realized something. The word 'Eagleton' kind of sounds like 'butt.' Eagleton. Butt-leton.

jokes.text: I'm April Ludgate Kevorkian.
jokes.setup: April introduces herself to a friendly orientation guide named Laura
jokes.punchline: April gives her last name as 'Kevorkian' — after Jack Kevorkian, the euthanasia doctor — as a dark joke to unsettle a new person, likely because she's in vet school
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical dark joke. 'Kevorkian' as April's new fake last name at vet school orientation is an ideal character moment — it's dark, contextually appropriate (vet = animal doctor = euthanasia adjacent), and delivered with complete seriousness. Near-perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Eagleton's in complete financial freefall. They're going to need a massive bailout just to survive the next fiscal year.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. This is terrible. This is... this is actually really hot.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I know people are suffering, but watching you problem-solve under pressure? It's doing things to me.

jokes.text: So you go with Laura, who seems really nice and does not deserve to be tortured.
jokes.setup: Ann sends April off with the friendly guide Laura
jokes.punchline: Ann feels the need to explicitly tell April not to torture Laura — the implication being that April absolutely would otherwise
jokes.explanation: A decent character comedy beat that acknowledges April's malevolence while characterizing Ann's exhausted maternal management of her. 'Does not deserve to be tortured' is the funny word choice — it's so resigned.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to recreate the Good Will Hunting scene. You know, 'It's not your fault.' I'll be Matt Damon, you be Robin Williams.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, no. That's not happening.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Come on! It's a beautiful scene. It's emotional, it's powerful.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm not sitting on a park bench while you cry at me about your childhood.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But that's what makes it great! Please, Ben. It's not your fault.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Stop.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's not your fault.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's not your fault. It's not your fault. It's not your fault.

jokes.text: Sure you wanna leave me here with her? What if I'm a murderer?
jokes.setup: Ann is about to leave April with Laura
jokes.punchline: April's parting shot is questioning whether Ann should trust her with a stranger — framed as April potentially being the threat, not the stranger
jokes.explanation: A quick, economical dark joke. April inverting the 'stranger danger' dynamic (she's the potential danger) is in character. The delivery as a legitimate concern she's raising is what makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That is the most absurd thing I've ever heard. You're telling me you have no power whatsoever? You're just a cog in the machine? That's a pathetic way to live.

jokes.text: Their debt-to-equity ratio is ridonkulous. / What a hilarious word. It reminds me of a ridiculous donkey.
jokes.setup: Ben describes Eagleton's terrible financial situation
jokes.punchline: Chris is delighted by the word 'ridonkulous' and immediately etymologizes it as 'ridiculous donkey' — technically correct and completely missing the point
jokes.explanation: Chris's enthusiastic, literal-minded deconstruction of slang is perfect character comedy. 'It reminds me of a ridiculous donkey' is an endearingly earnest response. Strong character integration — Chris's relentless positivity applied to linguistic analysis is very specifically him.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wow, look at all these baby products! Oh man, this one has a NASCAR driver on it. That's so cool!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Of course it does. This is Pawnee.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Every baby product in Pawnee features a NASCAR driver. Diapers, bottles, car seats... it's just what we do here.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's actually amazing.

jokes.text: Now that is the sexiest thing you've ever said to me. / Really, that?
jokes.setup: Ben reveals Eagleton is on the brink of financial disaster
jokes.punchline: Leslie repeats the exact phrase from the cold open ('That's the sexiest thing you've ever said to me'), but this time about Eagleton's bankruptcy — Ben's incredulous 'Really, that?' acknowledges the callback
jokes.explanation: A well-executed callback that also subverts itself — Ben's 'Really, that?' acknowledges the running bit while gently questioning it. The reuse of the phrase for Eagleton's impending bankruptcy rather than political rhetoric shows escalation of Leslie's feelings. The meta-awareness makes it better than a straight callback.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April? What are you doing here? You're supposed to be at orientation.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I was, but then I saw this store and remembered I needed baby stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So you just... left? That's a pretty big decision.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I decided I didn't want to go anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: When?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Just now. In the parking lot. I realized I could either go to orientation or come here. So I came here.

jokes.text: You pretend you're Ingrid. Let's pretend this box is the basket of apples I bet them on the game. / I see where you're going with this. / No, you don't. / Yeah, you're gonna ask me if I like apples-- / Do you like apples? / We just watched this movie two nights ago, so-- / Do you like apples? / I don't wanna do this. / How about them apples?
jokes.setup: Leslie sets up a 'Good Will Hunting' bit using the apples-and-oranges wager; Ben sees it coming immediately
jokes.punchline: Ben tries to dodge the entire sequence, but Leslie bulldozes through it anyway to deliver 'How about them apples?' — the joke is Ben's resigned tolerance of Leslie's dorky enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: The meta-structure here is the real joke: Ben sees the bit coming immediately and tries to skip it, but Leslie insists on performing it anyway. This is about their relationship as much as the pun. The extended refusal/insistence before the punchline makes the eventual 'How about them apples?' simultaneously a victory and a defeat.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: Sorry I'm late to the budget meeting. I was at a bankruptcy announcement.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: They had entertainment at their bankruptcy announcement.

jokes.text: Paul, if you ever see another one of these with my name on it, I want you to drive into the woods and bury it. / I don't decide who gets mail, sir. I just deliver it. / Passing the buck -- the last refuge of the cowardly and black-hearted. / That seems harsh. / Get out.
jokes.setup: Ron instructs the postal worker Paul about handling future junk mail
jokes.punchline: Paul reasonably explains he just delivers mail; Ron responds with a thunderous condemnation ('the last refuge of the cowardly and black-hearted') for the mildest possible bureaucratic deflection. 'That seems harsh' / 'Get out' completes it.
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron Swanson: the wildly disproportionate rhetorical response to a completely reasonable statement. 'The last refuge of the cowardly and black-hearted' for 'I just deliver mail' is magnificent. 'That seems harsh' from Paul is a perfect straight-man reaction, and 'Get out' closes it with maximum economy. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: Not having brunch? That's not civilized. That's barbaric.

jokes.text: Are you sure you want me to cut up this card? It gets you into the parking garage. / I'll be taking the bus now, and I'll be paying in cash.
jokes.setup: Ron is systematically eliminating all traces of himself from the grid, including cutting up his last credit card
jokes.punchline: The credit card is also a parking pass — Ron has just committed himself to taking the bus and paying cash as a matter of privacy principle
jokes.explanation: A decent escalation beat in the de-gridding sequence. Ron's immediate acceptance of the bus consequence is in character — he will not let practical inconvenience compromise his principles. Functional but not standout.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Why are we spending $50,000 on public pool renovations? That seems excessive.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: Well, Ben, I think of public pools as spas for poor people.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... that's not what a spa is, and that's definitely not what a pool is.

jokes.text: Isn't there a photo of you up at JJ's Diner, from that time when you-- aah! / Come on, Tom!
jokes.setup: Tom is about to remind Ron of a photo at JJ's Diner that would expose his existence
jokes.punchline: Ron apparently physically silences Tom mid-sentence — Tom's scream ('aah!') followed by Ron's weary 'Come on, Tom!' implies Ron grabbed him or covered his mouth; the violence of the privacy-protection is the joke
jokes.explanation: A physical gag inferred from 'aah!' — Ron grabs or startles Tom to stop him from saying the dangerous information out loud. The escalating lengths Ron will go to for privacy is the sustained joke of this subplot. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: It's not a waste, it's an investment in quality programming. As HBO used to say, 'It's not TV, it's HBO.'

jokes.text: These are the first bibs I've ever seen without Dale Earnhardt Jr.'s face on them.
jokes.setup: Ann is thrilled by a baby store in Bloomington that has everything she needs
jokes.punchline: Pawnee's baby bibs apparently all feature Dale Earnhardt Jr. — another entry in the Pawnee-is-terrible/Pawnee-is-very-specific running gag
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Dale Earnhardt Jr. on baby bibs is what makes this joke. It's not just 'redneck things' — it's a precise, absurd image. High economy (one sentence, complete world-building) and very quotable. The juxtaposition with Ann's sincere relief makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't have time to wait for eggs to cook. I'm a busy man.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: So I ate them raw. Shell and all.

jokes.text: I'm sorry we're late. We came from our bankruptcy brunch. And Michael Buble played, but he ran a little long.
jokes.setup: Ingrid arrives late to the financial recovery meeting
jokes.punchline: She was at a 'bankruptcy brunch' — a surreal but very Eagleton idea — and Michael Bublé performed but 'ran a little long.' The casualness of having a live celebrity performance at a casual brunch is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent world-building absurdism. 'Bankruptcy brunch' alone is funny — but the addition of Michael Bublé as entertainment who 'ran a little long' elevates it significantly. The specificity of Bublé (not a rock star, just a pleasant adult contemporary artist) is perfect. The casual complaint about his running long implies this is normal for them.

jokes.text: Was a bankruptcy brunch the best idea? / Sure, let's not have brunch... like animals.
jokes.setup: Ben questions whether a bankruptcy brunch was appropriate given their financial crisis
jokes.punchline: Ingrid's defense is that NOT having brunch would be living 'like animals' — the inversion of what constitutes civilized vs. animal behavior is the joke
jokes.explanation: The ellipsis-and-pivot structure of 'Sure, let's not have brunch... like animals' is excellent. The pause before 'like animals' does real work, making it land like a genuine philosophical position. High quotability. Strong Ingrid character integration — she is genuinely unable to conceive of voluntary austerity.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: This is my grandmother. Her name is Andy.

dialogue.speaker: College Guide
dialogue.line: Your grandmother?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yes. She's very old.

jokes.text: You filled the public pools with bottled water? / Total body hydration.
jokes.setup: Leslie reviews the questionable expenditures in Eagleton's budget
jokes.punchline: Eagleton filled public pools with bottled water; Ingrid's defense is 'Total body hydration' — delivered as an obvious, unanswerable justification
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of filling a public pool with bottled water is excellent — it's the most expensive possible way to fill a pool and also completely pointless (you don't drink pool water). 'Total body hydration' as a justification is the perfect three-word non-answer. Economy is great.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, what's up, homies? It's ya girl Grandma in the hizzouse!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Nobody says 'hizzouse' anymore, Andy. You're not even getting the decade right.

jokes.text: We purchased HBO for the whole town. / I'm sorry. You spent government money on a TV subscription? / It's not TV.
jokes.setup: Another Eagleton expenditure: they bought HBO for the entire town
jokes.punchline: When challenged, Ingrid responds with HBO's own famous slogan ('It's not TV') — using the premium cable justification in the context of government malfeasance
jokes.explanation: The HBO slogan repurposed as a sincere defense of government spending is sharp and economical. 'It's not TV' lands as both a direct HBO reference and a genuine expression of Eagleton's values — they really do think they're above regular TV. Double-layered joke with real economy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I wish you would die.

jokes.text: Let's get started with our first slide. 'Well, well, well...' Tsk, tsk, tsk.
jokes.setup: Leslie presents a financial recovery presentation to Eagleton officials
jokes.punchline: The first slide of a financial recovery presentation is apparently just the phrase 'Well, well, well...' with disapproving sound effects — Leslie has used government presentation time to mock Eagleton
jokes.explanation: The image of a professional financial recovery slide reading 'Well, well, well...' followed by Leslie doing audible tsk-tsks is a great visual/character joke. It perfectly captures Leslie's inability to maintain professionalism when Eagleton is involved. The tsk-tsks are what elevates it from funny to very funny.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I want to see where people have died. Like, the oldest graves in the cemetery, and maybe some of the buildings where famous people died. Oh, and if there's a spot where someone was hit by a car, I'd like to see that too.

jokes.text: JJ, a few months ago, I came in here and began eating eggs. They were delicious, so I ordered more. Before long, I believe I had eaten -- 51 eggs in 20 minutes. Couldn't cook 'em fast enough. The last ten were still in the shell.
jokes.setup: Ron has come to JJ's Diner to retrieve a public photo of himself
jokes.punchline: Ron casually recounts eating 51 eggs in 20 minutes as backstory — including 'the last ten were still in the shell' as a detail he seems unbothered by
jokes.explanation: An exceptional Ron Swanson moment. The escalation from 'I ordered eggs' to 51 eggs in 20 minutes to 'the last ten were still in the shell' is a perfect three-step comedy escalation. The complete casualness with which Ron reports this — as simple context for the story — is the key. This is Ron Swanson at his most mythological, which is his richest comic vein.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: As you can see from slide one, the Parks Department has made tremendous progress this year. Slide two shows our budget efficiency. And slide three... well, slide three is just a picture of Jerry with the caption 'Why.'

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What? Leslie!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Slide four demonstrates Tom's complete lack of business acumen. Slide five is Ben looking disappointed, which honestly is his default state. And slide six shows April's customer service skills, which I've rated as 'aggressively unhelpful.'

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This isn't helpful at all!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's the presentation, everyone. Questions?

jokes.text: Okay, but I don't know how anybody would know it's you. We followed your instructions.
jokes.setup: Ron asks for the photo of him at JJ's Diner to be destroyed
jokes.punchline: JJ implies the photo has been so modified (presumably per Ron's prior privacy instructions) that it's unrecognizable — implying Ron has been managing his diner photo documentation for years
jokes.explanation: A supporting beat for the Ron de-gridding plot. The implication that JJ has been accommodating Ron's privacy wishes for years is a nice world-building detail. Functional but not a standout joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, we need to merge with Eagleton, but we can do this without losing our identity. We just need to keep our eyes on the prize and stay the course.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not saying it'll be easy. But if we play our cards right and keep our nose to the grindstone, we can have our cake and eat it too.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Plus, I'll make sure we get someone really professional to oversee the whole thing. Like a butler, but for municipal government.

jokes.text: That's too much information. Let's go. / Where are we going now? / I've eaten a lot of food in a lot of restaurants. Why is everyone else so bad at eating?
jokes.setup: JJ says something about the photo that's 'too much information' (inaudible/cut); Ron declares they need to leave
jokes.punchline: Ron's parting philosophical observation: 'I've eaten a lot of food in a lot of restaurants. Why is everyone else so bad at eating?' — an absurd manifesto about his superiority as a food consumer
jokes.explanation: The Ron Swanson voice is perfectly captured: 'Why is everyone else so bad at eating?' is a question only Ron Swanson could ask with complete sincerity. It's delivered as genuine puzzlement, which is funnier than arrogance. The implicit claim that 51 eggs in the shell represents superior eating technique is the unstated joke underneath. High quotability, very strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: I'm just trying to live my truth in a post-modern, intersectional space.

jokes.text: As you remember, I'm April, and this is Ann, my 65-year-old grandmother. / Yes, that's who I am. Anyway...
jokes.setup: April and Ann have returned to the orientation after a deal; April has agreed to pretend Ann is her grandmother
jokes.punchline: Ann gamely accepts the premise ('Yes, that's who I am. Anyway...') — her resigned compliance with April's cruelty is the joke
jokes.explanation: A good cringe comedy beat — Ann's 'Yes, that's who I am. Anyway...' is a hilarious swallowing of pride. The joke is Ann's willingness to be humiliated for April's sake (and her own secret maternal investment in April). 'Anyway...' trying to move on is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, I've been live-tweeting Ron's entire attempt to go off the grid. We're up to 47,000 followers.

jokes.text: We'd love to hear about Bloomington. It seems like a real hip kind of college town. / Mee-maw, God, no one uses the word hip anymore.
jokes.setup: Ann (as 65-year-old grandmother) tries to engage with Laura about Bloomington using the word 'hip'
jokes.punchline: April, maintaining the bit, corrects 'Mee-maw' for using the outdated slang 'hip' — which is more embarrassing because April clearly can't stand Ann
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: April calling Ann 'Mee-maw' while also being condescending to her about the word 'hip' commits fully to the bit. Ann having to hear herself called Mee-maw is its own small punishment. Good cringe structure.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, you posted on Instagram.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I did not. I don't even know what that is.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, someone posted a photo of a wooden desk with the caption 'Finally got my workspace organized.'

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That was not me.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, it's from your account. And now I've posted about you posting. And I'm about to post about me posting about you posting. It's social media inception.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I need to lie down.

jokes.text: Sometimes I wish you went down on the Titanic with all your sorority sisters.
jokes.setup: April continues the bit of Ann being her elderly grandmother
jokes.punchline: April (as granddaughter) wishes 'Mee-maw' had died on the Titanic with her sorority sisters — the dark escalation of the bit beyond mere embarrassment into genuine cruelty
jokes.explanation: This is a great dark comedy line. The specific detail of 'sorority sisters on the Titanic' creates an absurd historical image while also being April's most pointed attack on Ann's persona (she's a sorority type). Delivered while Laura is right there makes it cringe-dark comedy. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Social media is a disease that has infected our society. People voluntarily surrendering their privacy, their time, their dignity, to corporations that monetize their existence. It's the death of civilization disguised as entertainment.

jokes.text: How are your local graveyards? I have some planning to do.
jokes.setup: Laura offers to show them around campus and asks what they'd like to see
jokes.punchline: April's request is to see the local graveyards because she has 'planning to do' — dark, absurd, and completely genuine in tone
jokes.explanation: Pure April. 'I have some planning to do' is the perfect follow-up — it implies not idle morbid interest but active death-related project planning. Economy is excellent. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's tight!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You know, my grandmother used that same expression. She's 127 years old.

jokes.text: Leslie reads her presentation slides to Eagleton: 'You blew it. / Super hard. / Complete buffoonery. / It's hilarious.' / And 'You deserve it.'
jokes.setup: Ben asks if Leslie wants to take it easy on Eagleton in her financial recovery presentation
jokes.punchline: The subsequent slides in her financial presentation are apparently just escalating insults: 'You blew it. Super hard. Complete buffoonery. It's hilarious. And you deserve it.' — Leslie has created a PowerPoint of mockery
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured escalation from the 'Well, well, well' first slide. Each subsequent slide is more damning: from insinuating to directly accusatory to a final 'You deserve it.' The escalation from 'Well, well, well' to 'Complete buffoonery' to 'You deserve it' is perfectly paced. Very strong character integration — Leslie's inability to separate her job from her feelings about Eagleton is the central joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Why does everyone keep throwing things at me?

jokes.text: We are willing to provide a bridge loan for $50,000. / 25% interest compounded monthly. / And you need to release a statement that says that Pawnee rules and Eagleton drools.
jokes.setup: Leslie presents the terms of Pawnee's bridge loan offer to Eagleton
jokes.punchline: After two legitimate financial terms, the third requirement is that Eagleton must release a statement saying 'Pawnee rules and Eagleton drools' — the playground insult as official government policy
jokes.explanation: The comedy of this is in the perfect structural fake-out: two legitimate financial terms (bridge loan, 25% interest) lead to the third term being 'Pawnee rules and Eagleton drools.' The descension from financial language to playground rhyme is exactly where the laugh lands. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It says 'Mo' Money, Mo' Problems' but it's about municipal bonds.

jokes.text: We have a saying in Eagleton: 'You don't kick a dressage horse after a failed pas de deux.'
jokes.setup: Ingrid tries to appeal to Leslie's sense of decency
jokes.punchline: The Eagletonian wisdom involves dressage horses and failed ballet duets — the proverb is technically coherent but absurdly rarefied, accessible only to people who do competitive equestrian ballet
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The Eagletonian proverb involving dressage horses and a pas de deux is a perfect distillation of the town's absurd elitism — their folk wisdom is about activities that 99% of people have never done. The proverb also makes a kind of abstract sense, which is funnier. High quotability and originality.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: I have a PhD!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: In what?

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: Fashion.

jokes.text: Whatever, blondie. Your butler made your bed, now you gotta lie in it.
jokes.setup: Ingrid cites Eagletonian wisdom; Leslie responds
jokes.punchline: Leslie modifies the idiom 'you made your bed, now lie in it' to 'your butler made your bed' — acknowledging that Eagletonians have butlers while landing the moral point
jokes.explanation: A well-executed idiom modification. 'Your butler made your bed, now you gotta lie in it' works both as a class joke and as a legitimate application of the proverb (they delegated, outsourced, and now face consequences). Clean, economical, and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, when two people get married, they become one person in the eyes of the law. So when you married me, you legally became me. Which means you agreed to everything I've ever agreed to, including the Eagleton boycott.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not how marriage works.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm pretty sure it is.

jokes.text: And if you walk out that door, none of us here, and I repeat, none of us will ever help you again. / Oh, my God. They have Michael Buble on retainer.
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers a dramatic ultimatum to Ingrid (evoking a classic movie trope)
jokes.punchline: Ben, who has presumably looked at the Eagleton budget, immediately spots that they have Michael Bublé on retainer — puncturing Leslie's dramatic moment with a mundane fiscal observation
jokes.explanation: The callback to Michael Bublé is well-earned — we now learn his appearance at the brunch wasn't a one-off but part of a retainer arrangement. The juxtaposition of Leslie's dramatic ultimatum with Ben's budget-discovery reaction is a perfect comedic beat. The discovery that they have a pop star on RETAINER recontextualizes the earlier joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What did you do?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I may have told your girlfriend that you cried during The Lion King.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What? You did cry. And it was relevant to the conversation.

jokes.text: Great news, Ron. Jean-Ralphio loves your shirt. / What the hell are you talking about? / Oh, I've been taking pictures of you all day for my new Facebook album: 'Ronswan: Gettin' off the grid.'
jokes.setup: Ron is deep in the process of removing himself from all digital records
jokes.punchline: Tom has been secretly photographing Ron all day and posting them to Facebook in an album called 'Ronswan: Gettin' off the grid' — the perfect ironic undoing of Ron's privacy mission
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully structured irony joke. The entire Ron subplot has been building toward a catastrophic privacy failure, and this is the perfect form of it: Tom, his employee, has been documenting Ron's anti-documentation efforts and posting them publicly. 'Ronswan: Gettin' off the grid' as the album title is a stroke of genius — it perfectly encapsulates Tom's obliviousness and self-satisfaction.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy would be the worst person I'd ever meet.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Guy Fieri exists, so that's not true.

jokes.text: Tom, do you maybe see a problem with what you've done? / I do now. Yes, sorry. / Erase. Erase. Erase. / Erase all pictures of Ron!
jokes.setup: Ron confronts Tom about the Facebook album
jokes.punchline: Tom's immediate comprehension ('I do now') followed by a frantic erasing sequence, culminating in Tom shouting 'Erase all pictures of Ron!' to others — the escalation from quiet confrontation to chaos
jokes.explanation: A solid escalation gag. Tom's instant comprehension ('I do now. Yes, sorry.') without defensiveness is funny, and 'Erase all pictures of Ron!' as a shouted order is a good escalation. Functional but not the highlight of the subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't believe you just fouled me like that! That was completely unnecessary!

dialogue.speaker: Basketball Player
dialogue.line: Yeah well, I'm the best player in this league, I'm a shooting machine, and I'm gonna take your team down, one basket at a time, baby!

jokes.text: What the hell is happening? / I think you accidentally opened up Vine. / You just vined your first selfie, Ron. / And I'm vining you vine your selfie. / The world is a nightmare.
jokes.setup: Ron tries to help erase photos and accidentally engages with Vine instead
jokes.punchline: Ron has accidentally made a Vine selfie; Tom responds by vining Ron making his Vine selfie — recursive social media documentation, topped by Ron's existential verdict: 'The world is a nightmare.'
jokes.explanation: This is the comedic peak of the Ron subplot. The recursive logic (vining someone vining their selfie) is absurdist escalation, and then 'The world is a nightmare' is one of the episode's most quotable lines — it's Ron's verdict on the entire digital age delivered as a complete philosophical conclusion. Maximum character integration, high economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I'm thinking of moving to Yucca Mountain.

dialogue.speaker: Diane Lewis
dialogue.line: Ron, that's a nuclear waste repository.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Exactly. It's remote, well-guarded, and completely isolated from society.

dialogue.speaker: Diane Lewis
dialogue.line: You know, every time something mildly inconveniences you, your solution is to move somewhere more remote. First it was that cabin, then it was Alaska, now it's literally a radioactive mountain.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Your point being?

dialogue.speaker: Diane Lewis
dialogue.line: My point is you have a problem.

jokes.text: Erase all pictures of Ron! (repeated in next scene)
jokes.setup: The 'erase all pictures of Ron' command has now apparently spread beyond Tom
jokes.punchline: The phrase appears to have become a rallying cry or command being issued to multiple people, implying the situation has snowballed
jokes.explanation: Running gag beat — the repetition of 'Erase all pictures of Ron' as a command implies the situation has escalated beyond Tom alone. Mild extension of the joke rather than a new punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, I know Eagletonians are attractive. That's the problem. It's stupid that they're attractive.

jokes.text: She said the B-line is cool, Mee-maw. Cool means good.
jokes.setup: Laura describes the B-line trail as 'cool'; Ann (as Mee-maw) presumably reacts
jokes.punchline: April translates 'cool' for her 'elderly grandmother' while being maximally condescending — the joke is April maintaining the grandmother bit while being rude to Ann
jokes.explanation: A functional beat in the April/Ann bit — the translation of 'cool means good' as condescending Mee-maw management is mildly funny but not especially original. The premise carries the joke more than the execution.

dialogue.speaker: Pawnee Citizen
dialogue.line: I'm tired of bailing out Eagleton! We already paid for their new library, their parks, their schools...

dialogue.speaker: Pawnee Citizen
dialogue.line: You know what? I didn't even pay my taxes last year. I just didn't do it. Nobody caught me.

jokes.text: Youngsters? Am I 65 years old?
jokes.setup: Ann tries to convince April that Bloomington is great, calling the students 'youngsters'
jokes.punchline: Ann immediately realizes she used the word 'youngsters' — the same kind of outdated word she was mocked for using as the fake grandmother — and catches herself
jokes.explanation: A nice structural callback — Ann uses dated slang again, this time catching herself. The self-aware 'Am I 65 years old?' is a good reaction beat that also acknowledges she has partially internalized the bit. Clean economy.

dialogue.speaker: Pawnee Citizen
dialogue.line: If we merge with Eagleton, what's next? Human-animal merger? Pretty soon I'm married to a horse!

jokes.text: Think fast. / Oh! / Why do people keep assuming I'm ready to catch things?
jokes.setup: Ben throws something at Chris again
jokes.punchline: Chris's lament — 'Why do people keep assuming I'm ready to catch things?' — reframes the first 'think fast' as not a one-off but a recurring experience for Chris, implying his whole life involves people throwing things at him
jokes.explanation: The callback to the opening 'think fast' joke is well-structured. 'Why do people keep assuming I'm ready to catch things?' implies this is a pattern in Chris's life, which adds a layer to an already good joke. The passive phrasing ('people keep assuming') is funnier than if he'd said 'why do you keep doing this.' Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Bertram
dialogue.line: The people of Pawnee are... poor.

jokes.text: Eagleton: No money, mo' problems.
jokes.setup: Leslie unveils her t-shirts for the basketball game
jokes.punchline: The Notorious B.I.G.'s 'Mo Money Mo Problems' reworked as an anti-Eagleton slogan for a high school basketball game — Leslie's thoroughness in her anti-Eagleton branding
jokes.explanation: The Biggie reference is deployed with good specificity — 'No money, mo' problems' is a clean inversion of the original that also accurately describes Eagleton's situation. Ben noting 'I do like a good internal rhyme' is a nice capper. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: Pawnee is the most generous town I've ever seen. You people are so giving and selfless.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: I mean, you're not sophisticated or educated, but your hearts are in the right place.

jokes.text: I do like a good internal rhyme.
jokes.setup: Leslie reveals the 'No money, mo' problems' t-shirts
jokes.punchline: Ben's response analyzes the slogan as a literary construction ('internal rhyme') rather than reacting to the political boldness — he's a government finance nerd who appreciates prosody
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy — five words that do a lot of work. Ben's literary appreciation of the t-shirt slogan sidesteps the political content entirely, which is very on-brand. It's the kind of joke that rewards paying attention to character.

dialogue.speaker: Zoe
dialogue.line: This phone is ancient.

dialogue.speaker: Diane
dialogue.line: Ancient? This thing is so old, even the prop department at the movie studio said, 'We can't use that, it looks too outdated.'

jokes.text: Just one second. / Yeah. / I'm just gonna help them out, okay? / Mm. / Just for an hour.
jokes.setup: Ben has been secretly helping Ingrid with her finances; Leslie catches him
jokes.punchline: Ben's increasingly pathetic negotiation ('just for an hour') mirrors the classic 'I'll be home by midnight... 2 AM... 3 AM' dynamic of a partner caught doing something wrong
jokes.explanation: A mild cringe comedy beat — Ben walking back his commitment in real time is relatable but not exceptional. The joke relies on audience familiarity with relationship dynamics rather than anything specifically Parks & Rec.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Is that a belt clip? Ron, no. No, that is not happening. That is a fashion emergency. You look like a divorced IT guy at a Best Buy.

jokes.text: What, Ann? I just stole your phone and texted every guy in it that the baby was theirs. It's not that big of a deal.
jokes.setup: Ann seems upset about something April did while Ann was driving
jokes.punchline: April casually reveals she texted all the men in Ann's phone claiming the baby was theirs — and characterizes it as 'not that big of a deal'
jokes.explanation: A great April-bomb. The specificity of texting every guy in the phone that the baby is theirs is a dark, targeted chaos move — and 'not that big of a deal' delivered with complete sincerity elevates it. High originality and character integration. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I think I'm having a contraction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Oh my God, we need to get you to a hospital!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: No, no, it's not that kind of contraction. I'm just realizing something about myself.

jokes.text: It was right about marrying Andy, and it was right when it told me that you would be the worst person I would ever meet in my life. And I've met Guy Fieri, Ann.
jokes.setup: April defends trusting her gut instinct; uses her gut being right about Ann as an example
jokes.punchline: The scale of 'worst person I would ever meet' is validated by the comparison: April has met Guy Fieri, and Ann is still worse
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single best joke. The structure is perfect: the gut was right about marrying Andy (warm), right about Ann being terrible (harsh), and then the devastating calibration — 'And I've met Guy Fieri, Ann.' Guy Fieri is the perfect celebrity to cite as a baseline for unpleasantness: it's not mean (he's just loud and over-the-top) but it's specific and unmistakable. The pause implied by 'And I've met Guy Fieri, Ann.' — the repetition of Ann's name as a period — is devastating. Maximum character integration, high originality, flawless economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The contamination is worse than E. coli.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: What could be worse than E. coli?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's full of... apples.

jokes.text: Well, right now my gut is saying that we are going to listen to Mariah Carey the whole way home. / Good.
jokes.setup: April sarcastically tells Ann to 'just listen when your gut says something'; Ann decides to apply this advice
jokes.punchline: Ann's gut says to play Mariah Carey the whole way home — a petty but perfectly calibrated revenge. April's 'Good' suggests she likes Mariah, undermining Ann's attempted revenge.
jokes.explanation: A good tag for the April/Ann car scene. Ann's 'revenge' via Mariah Carey is thwarted by April actually liking it — the reversal is a nice beat. The warmth underneath April and Ann's relationship begins to show, which is the emotional throughline of their subplot.

jokes.text: I mean, they're 50 points ahead, and they're still dunking. I mean, look at this guy. There's no way he is in high school.
jokes.setup: Leslie is upset at the basketball game watching Eagleton dominate
jokes.punchline: Leslie's complaint that an Eagleton player is physically impossible to be in high school — the implication that Eagleton cheats by having adult players, or simply that Eagleton's superior resources extend to having basketball-playing giants
jokes.explanation: A functional joke during the game sequence. The observation is relatable but not especially original or specific enough to be standout. Part of a longer complaint sequence.

jokes.text: And I'm better at French horn too, Eric.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trash-talking the Eagleton team at the basketball game
jokes.punchline: She seemingly breaks into a random non sequitur about being better at French horn than someone named Eric — presumably an Eagletonian
jokes.explanation: A great non sequitur that implies a much larger history of Leslie vs. Eric (Eagletonian) rivalry beyond basketball. The specificity of French horn and the direct address to 'Eric' suggests years of competition we haven't seen. Economy is excellent — one sentence, big implied world.

jokes.text: And I'm better at French horn too, Eric.
jokes.setup: Leslie is watching Eagleton run up the basketball score
jokes.punchline: Leslie randomly calls out 'Eric' for being better at French horn — a completely out-of-context comeback to someone not involved in the current discussion
jokes.explanation: A fantastic throwaway. The joke implies Leslie has a long-running rivalry with someone named Eric that extends to French horn — a very specific, very petty grievance that surfaces in a completely unrelated context. The randomness is the point, and it's extremely quotable and revealing of Leslie's obsessive competitive nature. Good economy.

jokes.text: I don't see what the problem is. I will give you a certain amount of gold in exchange for a recreational vehicle. / I still need an address for insurance purposes. / This will be my new home. The address is wherever it is parked.
jokes.setup: Ron is buying an RV, intending to pay in gold and live in it
jokes.punchline: Ron is paying in gold bullion for an RV he intends to live in, and his 'address' is 'wherever it is parked' — total commitment to off-grid nomadic existence
jokes.explanation: Strong Ron moment. Paying in gold for an RV is perfectly Ron (cash, untraceable, physical), and the address being 'wherever it is parked' is the logical extension of his philosophy. Both elements work together to create the maximum version of off-grid Ron.

jokes.text: I've been busy destroying most of my personal effects and threatening a postal worker.
jokes.setup: Diane is upset that Ron was unreachable when she had a flat tire
jokes.punchline: Ron's explanation of what he was doing during her emergency: destroying personal effects and threatening a postal worker — delivered as reasonable activities that explain the lapse
jokes.explanation: The list format works perfectly — 'destroying most of my personal effects and threatening a postal worker' is delivered as if these are reasonable explanations. The escalation from 'destroying effects' (strange) to 'threatening a postal worker' (alarming) in a casual list is very funny. High character integration and economy.

jokes.text: You can't just roam the streets in an RV and be impossible to find. / I'm on a mission to get off the grid. / Well, you don't have to be entirely on the grid, but you have to be on our grid.
jokes.setup: Diane confronts Ron about being unreachable during an emergency
jokes.punchline: Diane's compromise: 'our grid' — the public grid is negotiable, but the family grid is non-negotiable
jokes.explanation: A warm, character-specific resolution to the Ron subplot. 'Our grid' is a beautifully economical way to articulate the balance between Ron's privacy principles and his family responsibilities. The joke works emotionally as well as comedically, which is Parks and Rec at its best.

jokes.text: I suppose you wouldn't consider moving. / I love you, but your solution to every problem is to live inside a mountain. / I love you too.
jokes.setup: Ron is processing the 'our grid' compromise from Diane
jokes.punchline: Ron suggests moving (presumably to a mountain); Diane calls him out: 'your solution to every problem is to live inside a mountain' — implying this is a recurring suggestion
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Your solution to every problem is to live inside a mountain' is a perfect summary of Ron Swanson as a character — delivered with love and exasperation by Diane. The 'I love you too' response from Ron (which doesn't address the mountain critique at all) is the ideal response. This line encapsulates their relationship brilliantly.

jokes.text: I suppose you wouldn't consider moving. / I've heard the school system in the tunnels beneath Yucca Mountain is adequate.
jokes.setup: Ron and Diane resolve the grid argument; Ron makes one final attempt to propose an alternative living arrangement
jokes.punchline: Ron has apparently researched the schooling options in nuclear waste tunnels under Yucca Mountain as a family home
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Ron researching the school district in the tunnels UNDER A NUCLEAR WASTE MOUNTAIN as a family home option — and describing it as merely 'adequate' — is pitch-perfect. The specificity (Yucca Mountain, not just 'a mountain'; 'tunnels beneath'; 'adequate' as damning with faint praise) elevates it to exceptional. Diane's 'I love you, but your solution to every problem is to live inside a mountain' is the perfect response. Justifies 8+ easily.

jokes.text: The magic phone scene: two large children's toy phones / Ew, gross, it has 'buttons.' / A cell phone belt clip? / No, Ron. Oh, my God! / Yeah, I can't be seen with you.
jokes.setup: Ron's solution for staying connected to family while being off the grid: children's toy phones given to Diane's kids, and a flip phone with a belt clip
jokes.punchline: The children mock the phone having 'buttons'; Tom and Donna are horrified by the belt clip; Ron loses their endorsement
jokes.explanation: A visual gag sequence — the toy phones, the old-school flip phone, the belt clip. 'I can't be seen with you' as Tom's final verdict on the belt clip is a good closer. Probably plays better visually than on the page; the transcript suggests the physical comedy carries the scene.

jokes.text: I love you, but your solution to every problem is to live inside a mountain.
jokes.setup: Ron proposes living in Yucca Mountain tunnels
jokes.punchline: Diane's deadpan observation that Ron's universal problem-solving methodology is 'live inside a mountain'
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect joke. Diane identifies Ron's pattern — his solution to EVERY problem is to retreat into a mountain — delivered with love but devastating accuracy. The phrase 'your solution to every problem is to live inside a mountain' is one of the most quotable lines in the episode. Diane's character is enriched by this — she loves Ron AND sees him clearly. Maximum economy. Justifies 8+ clearly.

jokes.text: I mean, did you steal this from a museum? Maybe find it frozen in ice? It looks like the original phone from the movie Wall Street. / I think it's just the original phone, period.
jokes.setup: Tom and Donna look at Ron's ancient flip phone
jokes.punchline: Donna's correction — it's not just like the Wall Street phone, it IS the original phone — implying Ron has an actual decades-old phone still in operation
jokes.explanation: Tom's riff on the ancient phone (museum/frozen in ice/Wall Street) is good, but Donna's single-line correction — 'I think it's just the original phone, period' — is the punchline that lands. The Straight-man close is more economical than the setup.

jokes.text: Eagleton is terrible! Why should I bail them out with the hard-earned money from my unemployment check?
jokes.setup: Citizens are angry at the proposal to help Eagleton
jokes.punchline: The speaker is on unemployment — their 'hard-earned money' is a government payment, making their stand against government spending paradoxical
jokes.explanation: A sharp political joke embedded in the townhall sequence. The irony of someone on unemployment opposing government spending is pointed without being preachy. Good structure and economy.

jokes.text: No one bailed me out when I got arrested for arson.
jokes.setup: Citizens continue objecting to the merger
jokes.punchline: Another citizen draws a false analogy between municipal financial bailouts and not being bailed out after committing arson — the casual disclosure of felony is the joke
jokes.explanation: A great crowd joke — the casual 'when I got arrested for arson' creates a perfect Pawnee citizen moment. The argument is both logically bonkers and delivered as completely reasonable. Economy is strong.

jokes.text: You can't just merge two towns. It's against the rules of nature. What's next -- merging a man with his dog?
jokes.setup: Citizens object to the town merger
jokes.punchline: The slippery slope argument goes directly to merging a man with his dog — the specific, strange escalation reveals the citizen's particular fears
jokes.explanation: A good Pawnee citizen moment. The slippery slope argument jumping directly to man-dog merging is absurdist but consistent with Pawnee's chaotic townhall tradition. The specificity of 'his dog' (possessive, implying a particular fear) is a nice touch.

jokes.text: I live in Eagleton. And frankly, I don't like the idea of living in Pawnee. They're a little -- oh, what's the word? / Have-no-money.
jokes.setup: An Eagletonian at the meeting complains about the prospect of being merged into Pawnee
jokes.punchline: Ingrid provides the word: 'Have-no-money' — a hyphenated compound adjective that is essentially Eagleton's contempt for Pawnee distilled, delivered by someone who is now also broke
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. 'Have-no-money' as a class epithet delivered by someone who is actively bankrupt is sharp irony. The phrasing as a hyphenated compound adjective is inventive — it feels like Eagletonian usage, as if this is their actual word for poor people. Ingrid delivering it makes it funnier given her situation.

jokes.text: First of all, Eagleton has no money. Second of all, they are gracious enough to throw us a lifeline, and we should be eternally grateful for their generosity. They're a town of angels -- greasy, denim-clad angels, but angels nonetheless.
jokes.setup: Ingrid tries to convince her own constituents to accept the merger with Pawnee
jokes.punchline: Ingrid calls Pawnee a 'town of angels' — then can't quite commit, adding 'greasy, denim-clad angels, but angels nonetheless.' The concession is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A strong character-flip moment for Ingrid. The structure of 'town of angels — greasy, denim-clad angels, but angels nonetheless' is beautifully balanced — she gives with one hand and takes back with the other, which reveals she still can't fully transcend her elitism even in a moment of genuine gratitude. 'Greasy, denim-clad' is the perfect qualifier. High quotability.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. I'm having one. / A contraction? / No. Dude, I'm, like, three months pregnant. I-I know. I'm just so excited. / The thing I'm having is a gut feeling.
jokes.setup: Ann makes an announcement with dramatic urgency while in a baby supplies store
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately assumes medical emergency (contraction) — but Ann is just having a 'gut feeling.' The misdirect plays on her pregnancy to generate a false alarm.
jokes.explanation: A well-structured misdirect using the pregnancy setup to generate a false medical alarm. 'No. Dude, I'm, like, three months pregnant' is a perfectly timed deflation. The callback to the gut feeling theme of the April/Ann subplot gives it thematic weight. Good structure.

jokes.text: I hate Eagletonians as much as you do. I hate their stupid beautiful faces and their stupid shiny hair.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to convince Pawnee citizens to accept the merger with Eagleton
jokes.punchline: Leslie's argument for helping Eagleton begins with validation of hating them — and her specific grievances are their physical attractiveness ('stupid beautiful faces,' 'stupid shiny hair')
jokes.explanation: A great Leslie moment. Her anti-Eagleton argument opens with shared hatred and specifically cites their physical attractiveness as a genuine grievance. 'Stupid beautiful faces' is the kind of specificity that makes a joke. Good character integration — Leslie can't help herself.

jokes.text: On the bright side, we did win the basketball game. / I think you owe us some apples. / You better pay up. / Oh, you don't want them. All of Pawnee's apples have been recalled -- g. Coli. / You mean e. Coli? / I wish. Way easy to treat. Welcome to Pawnee!
jokes.setup: The merger is settled; Ingrid acknowledges Pawnee won the game and owes them apples
jokes.punchline: All of Pawnee's apples have been recalled due to 'g. Coli' — a new, worse strain than e. Coli, delivered with 'Way easy to treat' as sarcastic understatement before the triumphant 'Welcome to Pawnee!'
jokes.explanation: A perfect episode closer. The callback to the apple wager is beautifully structured: now that we care about Pawnee winning, the apples are recalled — not with e. Coli but with the fictional 'g. Coli' (funnier, implies it's even more obscure and serious). 'I wish. Way easy to treat.' is a brilliant deadpan. 'Welcome to Pawnee!' as the final button on the episode perfectly encapsulates the show's affectionate-but-honest portrait of the town. High impact as a closing joke.

jokes.text: You better pay up. / Oh, you don't want them. All of Pawnee's apples have been recalled — g. Coli. / You mean e. Coli? / I wish. Way easy to treat. / Welcome to Pawnee!
jokes.setup: Leslie demands her apples from the wager
jokes.punchline: Pawnee's apples have been recalled due to 'g. Coli' — a new, presumably worse pathogen than e. Coli; Leslie's 'I wish' about e. Coli being 'way easy to treat' is a perfect dark button; 'Welcome to Pawnee!' is the ideal episode closer
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and one of the strongest in the series' comedic toolkit. The payoff works on multiple levels: (1) Callback to the apple wager, (2) 'g. Coli' as a completely made-up and somehow worse pathogen than e. Coli, (3) Leslie's 'I wish' framing e. Coli as the GOOD outcome, (4) the existential acceptance of 'Way easy to treat' implying they've dealt with worse, (5) 'Welcome to Pawnee!' as the perfect civic pride button. This is the series' self-aware joke about its own world-building done at peak efficiency. Justifies 8.7 easily — it's exceptional structure, exceptional character integration, and extraordinarily quotable.

tmdb_overview: Leslie pairs up the Pawnee Parks employees with their Eagleton counterparts. Meanwhile Ben and Chris reunite for an accounting project, and Ann reveals her plans for the future.
insight: Sports rivalry escalates through character absurdity, but 76 score reflects uneven pacing across 66 jokes.
